docs.title: Welcome to Text Lab
docs.text:
Text Lab is an interactive platform designed to make advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) tools accessible to researchers and students at the University of Bern.

Developed by the Data Science Lab (DSL), Text Lab allows you to process documents, audio, and data without needing to write code.

docs.title: Data Privacy & Security
docs.text:
Why use Text Lab?

One of the primary advantages of Text Lab is data sovereignty

  • Internal Processing: All processing happens within the University of Bern's infrastructure: on the UBELIX compute node of your session, or, only if you choose the GPUStack option in the Knowledge Graph, on the university's GPUStack service.
  • No Third Parties: Unlike commercial cloud services (like ChatGPT or Google Cloud), your data is never sent to external servers.
  • Nothing Left Behind: Files you upload and intermediate results are kept in a private workspace for your session, which only your user account can open, and are deleted when the session ends. What you keep is up to you: the files you download, and the output folder you choose in the Knowledge Graph. Each session also keeps technical log files in your home directory (see Reporting a Problem).
  • Sensitive Data: Text Lab is the better choice for working with potentially sensitive research data (e.g., for interviews and/or non-public documents).
  • No coding required Text lab offers advanced NLP models and tools without having to write code.

docs.title: Available Tools
docs.text:
• Transcription: Convert audio files to text with high accuracy, featuring a specialized model for Swiss German.
  • OCR (Optical Character Recognition): Extract text from scanned PDFs using state-of-the-art AI models.
    • Historic German handwriting: a section of the OCR tool that transcribes handwritten historical German documents (Kurrent, medieval hands) line by line, with models of the University of Bern's Digital Humanities group.
    • Hugging Face OCR models: a section of the OCR tool that reads documents with a vision-language model of your choice from Hugging Face, downloaded into your own folder.
  • Translate: Securely translate text and complex documents while preserving formatting.
  • Meeting Notes Generator: Automatically transcribe and summarize audio recordings into structured notes, with each point linked to the part of the transcript it comes from.
  • Chat: Interact with local Large Language Models (LLMs) securely.
  • Data Visualization: Generate insights and plots from your data.
  • Knowledge Graphs: Extract metadata from research papers and visulise the data with knowledge graphs.
  • Topic Modeling: Apply unsupervised algorithem to raw text data to discover topics and trends.

For processing large amount of data, please contact the Data Science Lab.

docs.title: Getting Support
docs.text:
If you encounter issues, need any data science, research IT support, or have questions about using Text Lab, please contact the Data Science Lab. When reporting a problem, please attach the session's log files (how to find them): support.dsl@unibe.ch

If you'd like to be informed about updates and changes to Text Lab, please subscribe to the following Mailing List

docs.title: General Disclaimer (Applies to All Features)
docs.text:
The use of Text Lab and its featured tools is provided "AS IS."

While we strive for accuracy, most of the results are AI-generated and are intended for informational and drafting purposes only.

Users are solely responsible for verifying all data, transcripts, translations, and summaries before relying on them for critical decisions, legal action, or professional reporting.

docs.title: Chat
docs.text:
Chat lets you talk to large language models (LLMs) that run on the university cluster. You can ask questions, brainstorm research ideas, draft and edit text, or upload documents to summarise, translate or question them. If you upload a table, Chat can also create plots and run statistical tests on it.

Your messages and files never leave the university network. Nothing is sent to external services such as OpenAI, Google or Anthropic.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Choose a model in the sidebar under Model Selection. If you are unsure, keep the first one.
  2. Attach files (optional) under Upload Context: up to 4 documents or tables.
  3. Type your message in the box at the bottom of the page and press Enter.
  4. Wait for the first reply. The first message loads the model into GPU memory, which can take 1–2 minutes. Later replies start within seconds.
  5. Download Conversation (.md) in the sidebar to keep the conversation.

Click Start New Chat to clear the conversation and begin again. Download anything you want to keep first: a cleared conversation cannot be restored.

docs.title: How much the model can read
docs.text:
A model reads a limited amount of text at once, its context window. Your whole conversation and your attached files are sent with every message, so a conversation fills the window as it grows. The sidebar shows how full it is, for example Context used: ~6,200 of ~21,000 tokens (30%). A token is a piece of a word; 1,000 tokens are roughly 750 English words. The number is an estimate.

  • Answers get less reliable as the window fills, well before it is full: the model pays less attention to details in a long conversation. From 75% on, the sidebar suggests starting a new chat.
  • When the window is full, the model no longer sees the oldest messages, and the sidebar says so. Start a new chat; if you need earlier results, paste a short summary of them into your first message.
  • Long attached files are read in parts (see below), so they do not fill the window on their own. A new chat does not help with those, so the sidebar does not suggest it for them.

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
The models available depend on the GPU your Text Lab session runs on. The sidebar shows the mode:

  • Standard Mode: smaller models only. They answer quickly and are fine for most everyday tasks.
  • High-Performance Mode (large GPUs such as the A100 or H100): all models, including large ones that give better answers for complex questions, at the cost of slower replies.

You can switch models at any time; the conversation continues with the new model. Models differ in strengths, so if one gives poor answers for your task, try another.

docs.title: Working with documents
docs.text:
Attach files in the sidebar under Upload Context. Attached files are included with every message you send, until you remove them.

File type What Chat does with it PDF (.pdf) Reads the text of the document Text (.txt) Reads the text (UTF-8) JSON (.json) Reads the text, and enables data analysis if it holds a table CSV, TSV, Excel (.csv, .tsv, .xlsx, .xls) Reads the first 100 rows as a table, and enables data analysis on the whole table
  • Limits: up to 4 files, each up to 10 MB. Larger files are skipped with a warning.
  • Files Chat cannot read are skipped with a warning above the answer, for example damaged or password-protected PDFs and text files that are not UTF-8.
  • Scanned PDFs contain images of text rather than text, so Chat cannot read them and says so. Convert them with OCR first.
  • Long documents are handled automatically. When a document is too long for the model to read at once (roughly 15,000 words, about 30 pages), Chat splits it into parts, answers your question for each part, and then combines the answers. You see the progress as Analyzing document part 2 of 5. This takes longer, and questions about details spread across the whole document are answered less precisely than for shorter documents.

Ask specific questions

"Summarise the methods section of study.pdf in five bullet points" gives a better answer than "What is this about?". Name the file when you have attached several.

docs.title: Analysing data in Chat
docs.text:
When you attach a table, the sidebar shows Data tools enabled for your file. You can then ask for plots or statistics in plain language, for example:

  • "Plot the distribution of age."
  • "Is income different between men and women?"
  • "Which variables are most strongly correlated with the outcome?"

For each message, Chat decides whether it needs the data tools. If it does, an activity log (Analysing your data...) shows the progress, and the answer contains a summary, the plots, the statistical results and the Python code that reproduces them. All other messages are answered as normal chat.

The analysis uses the same engine as Visualize Data; see there for the available plots and tests and how to read the results.

  • If you attach several tables, only the first one is analysed.
  • Analyses use the whole table, up to 300,000 rows.

Ask for statistics, not mental arithmetic

In normal chat the model only sees the first 100 rows of a table, so it cannot reliably answer questions such as "What is the average income?". Ask for a statistic or a plot instead ("Compute the mean income per region"), which uses the data tools on the complete table.

For more control, such as choosing columns, getting R code or downloading a full report, use Visualize Data.

docs.title: Saving your conversation
docs.text:
The sidebar offers downloads once the conversation has started:

  • Download Conversation (.md): the whole conversation as a Markdown text file, including any code.
  • Download with Plots (.html): appears when an analysis has produced plots. Contains the conversation together with the charts and opens in any web browser.

The conversation is lost when you click Start New Chat, reload the page, close the browser tab, or when your Text Lab session ends.

docs.title: Data privacy and security
docs.text:
You may be uploading sensitive, unpublished or proprietary research data to Chat. Text Lab is designed to keep it confidential. Here is exactly what happens to your data, and the technology behind it.

  • Documents are processed in memory. Documents you attach for the conversation (PDF, text, and tables read as text) are processed entirely in the server's temporary working memory (RAM). They are not saved, copied or written to your university home directory.
    • Technical transparency: the app uses Streamlit's uploaded_file.getvalue() to read the file into RAM. PDFs are read with PyMuPDF (fitz.open(stream=...)), tables with pandas from a memory buffer (pd.read_csv(BytesIO(...))).
  • Tables for data analysis are stored privately and temporarily. So that the analysis tools can read a table, Chat saves a copy of the first attached table, together with the plots created from it, in your session's private workspace on the compute node. Only your user account can open it, nothing is written to your home directory, and they are deleted when you click Start New Chat, and in any case when your Text Lab session ends.
  • Ephemeral sessions. Your conversation is kept only in your open browser tab (Streamlit's st.session_state). When you click Start New Chat, reload the page, close the browser, or your HPC job ends, the conversation is permanently deleted.
  • No AI training. The models run locally on the UBELIX compute nodes via Ollama. They only read your data to answer your current question (inference). The models do not learn from your data, and your data is never used to train or improve them.
  • Network isolation. All data stays within the University of Bern's secure HPC network. Nothing is ever sent to external services such as OpenAI, Google or Anthropic.

Large file uploads and temporary storage

Chat accepts documents of up to 10 MB, to keep them within what the model can read. The Text Lab server itself accepts much larger files (up to 10 GB) to support the Visualize Data and Knowledge Graph tools.

If you upload a very large file to Chat, the web framework (Streamlit) may temporarily store it in the session's temporary directory ($TMPDIR, inside the private session workspace) to avoid running out of memory, before Chat rejects it for being too large. That directory is deleted when the session ends.

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• AI answers can be wrong. Language models can produce inaccurate, misleading or invented statements that sound convincing. Check important facts, quotes and numbers against your sources.
  • No internet access. The models cannot browse the web, and their knowledge ends at the date they were trained.
  • No memory between chats. Each conversation starts from scratch. The model only knows what is in the current conversation and the attached files.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Click a problem to see what to do.

'Could not connect to Ollama server'

The service that runs the models is not available, usually because your Text Lab session has just started. Wait a minute and reload the page. If the message stays, end your session and start a new one.

The first reply takes a long time

The model is being loaded into GPU memory, which takes 1–2 minutes the first time you use it (the page shows Loading ... into GPU memory). Replies are fast afterwards. Switching to another model loads that model.

'File ... exceeds the 10MB limit. Skipped.'

Shorten the document or attach only the relevant part. To analyse a large table, use Visualize Data, which accepts much larger files.

'File ... contains no text, probably because it is scanned'

The PDF holds images of pages rather than text. Convert it with OCR and attach the result.

'File ... could not be read'

The file is damaged, password-protected, or (for text and JSON files) not saved as UTF-8. Open it, save it again (as UTF-8 for text), and attach it again.

My request for a plot or statistic was answered as normal chat

Check that the sidebar shows Data tools enabled for your table. Then ask explicitly for the plot or test, for example "Make a histogram of age" or "Run a t-test of income by sex".

'The analysis could not be started. The model produced a tool call Ollama could not parse'

Some models occasionally produce instructions that the system cannot read, especially with certain data. Select another model in the sidebar and ask again.

'The model did not answer within 300 seconds'

The model server was busy or stuck. Ask again, or try another model. If nothing responds any more, end your Text Lab session and start a new one.

'Ollama ResponseError'

The model server reported an error. Try again or choose another model. If the error keeps appearing, contact the Data Science Lab and include the message shown.

For help with your project, contact the Data Science Lab (DSL).

docs.title: Knowledge Graph
docs.text: Explore connections between scientific papers, authors, research topics and citations. Create a project with one build action, or open saved results to continue exploring in a later session.

docs.title: Create a project
docs.text:
1. Choose Create a project.
  2. Under Add papers, choose Upload PDF or ZIP (the default) or Use a folder on this cluster.
  3. For uploads, select one PDF or a ZIP containing PDF papers and enter a Project name. For a cluster folder, enter the folder containing PDFs.
  4. Choose Save project in: persistent storage on the cluster where you want the extracted results to remain. This path refers to the cluster, not your computer. By default, projects are saved beside the selected papers folder, or in your home directory for uploads. You can change either location. The full project folder path is displayed below it.
  5. To change how topics are extracted, open Advanced settings. Under Topic extraction mode, choose to run the language model in your Text Lab session (Ollama, no API key needed) or use the university's GPUStack service (API key required). The model reads paper titles and abstracts to identify research topics. With GPUStack, these are sent to the university service; with Ollama, they stay in your session. Session model choices follow the same GPU-based configuration as the other Text Lab features; the first configured model is selected by default.
  6. Click Build knowledge graph.

Text Lab extracts text, metadata and citations using Grobid, extracts research topics from titles and abstracts using the selected model, and opens the graph. Progress is shown while processing runs. The saved folder is <project name>_project_corpus for uploads or <PDF folder name>_project_corpus for cluster folders, under your chosen save location.

ZIPs may contain subfolders; only PDF papers are processed. Filenames are preserved, including in selectors such as P0001 - Paper.pdf. Each paper in a ZIP must have a unique filename, even across subfolders. Rename duplicates before uploading. Invalid archives and files without a PDF header show an error.

Uploaded PDFs are staged in the private job workspace and removed after the build attempt, including on failures. Extracted text, metadata, topics and graphs remain in your chosen project folder. To retry failed PDFs later, upload the original PDF or ZIP again using the same project name and save location. You do not need the original upload to open saved extractions or graphs.

PDF extractions are saved as processing progresses. Papers already extracted are recognised by PDF filename and reused; failed papers are retried. Changing a PDF without changing its filename does not trigger PDF extraction again. When you build or update a graph, topic extraction runs again for every paper with an abstract, including reused papers. The saved topic table is replaced only when extraction completes. Papers without abstracts are included without research topics.

If processing fails, the saved extractions remain available for another attempt.

docs.title: Open an existing project
docs.text:
Choose Open an existing project and enter either the project folder or a folder containing your saved projects. Select a project and click Open project. The source PDFs, Grobid server and topic model service are not needed to explore completed results.

Once a project is open, its save location is shown above the results. Use Choose another project to switch collections.

docs.title: How the graph is built
docs.text:
Stage Method What it gives you Read the PDFs Grobid extracts metadata, text and references from each PDF. Paper titles, authors, abstracts and citations, when available. Extract topics The selected language model reads each paper's title and abstract. It is asked for 3–8 specific topics, each with a broader category and a confidence score. Research themes for individual papers. Papers without an abstract skip this stage. Build and display the network NetworkX builds a directed graph from the extracted data. Pyvis uses a Barnes–Hut force layout to spread out nodes and draw connected nodes together. An interactive view of authorship, topics and citations.

Topic extraction works paper by paper. To discover groups of documents across a corpus using BERTopic, Top2Vec or LDA, use Topic Modeling. The distances between nodes in the Knowledge Graph are a result of the layout; they do not measure similarity.

docs.title: Understanding the results
docs.text: The saved project has three tabs: Explore, Papers, and Topics. Use them together: find a connection in the graph, identify the papers behind it, and check the topics the model assigned.

docs.title: Explore: the interactive graph
docs.text:
Use Whole collection to see links across your papers, or Single paper to focus on one paper and its connections. In Advanced graph options, you can choose node types to show, select papers for the whole collection view, and set a minimum topic confidence. The graph updates as you change these controls.

Hover over nodes for details. Drag the background to pan, zoom in or out within the graph, or use Recenter to fit all nodes back into view. The graph stays visible when unrelated controls cause the page to refresh.

In Whole collection, click any node to highlight the nodes one connection away and the links to them. For example, click a topic to see which papers are assigned to it. Other nodes fade. Click empty space to clear the highlight.

Below the graph, Nodes counts all displayed entities, Connections counts the links between them, and Papers counts the blue paper nodes. Separate citation nodes do not count towards Papers. These numbers describe the current view, so they can change when you apply filters.

docs.title: Colours, shapes, and connections
docs.text:
Each shape is a node. The same colour can mean different things when paired with different shapes, so look at both.

Node Colour and shape What it means Paper in your collection Blue circle A paper you added. The label is its project ID, such as P0001. Hover to see its title and DOI, if available. Author Green triangle An author of a paper in your collection. A shared author can connect several papers. Category Purple rectangle A broad research area, such as Computer Vision. Topic Red ellipse A specific theme within a category, such as Object Detection Networks. Topics are the more specific level; categories are the broader level. Cited paper in your collection Purple circle in Single paper A reference matched to a paper in your collection by title. In Whole collection, the citation connects to the paper's existing blue node. External cited paper Orange circle A reference that was not matched to a paper in the collection shown. Cited author Gold triangle An author whose work is cited by a paper in the graph. A citation does not imply co-authorship.

Read the labels on the connections to see why two nodes are linked:

  • authored or authored_by: an author wrote the paper.
  • has_topic: the model assigned this topic to the paper.
  • belongs_to: the specific topic belongs to the broader category.
  • in_category: the paper has a topic in that category.
  • cites: the paper references another paper.
  • cites_work_by: the paper references work by that author.

For example, if P0001 and P0002 both connect to the red topic Object Detection Networks, the model assigned the same topic label to both papers. If they only share the purple category Computer Vision, they share a broader research area and may have different specific topics. Neither connection means that one paper cites the other; look for a cites connection for that.

In Single paper, a larger topic node indicates higher model confidence. In Whole collection, topics grow with the number of times they appear; hover over a topic to see its average confidence.

docs.title: Papers: extracted metadata
docs.text: The Papers tab lists each paper's project ID, title, authors, publication date, and PDF filename. Use the ID to match a graph node such as P0001 to its source file. If you need the extracted abstract, DOI, or references, download the paper table as CSV.

docs.title: Topics: labels assigned to each paper
docs.text:
The Topics tab lists one row per topic assigned to a paper. The same topic can appear on multiple rows if it was assigned to multiple papers.

Field How to read it Paper The title of the paper the model read. Label The specific topic assigned to the paper, shown as a red ellipse in the graph. Category The broader research area containing the topic, shown as a purple rectangle. Confidence The model's estimate of the match on a scale from 0 to 1. Use it to filter suggestions, and check the abstract before relying on a label. It is not a validated accuracy score. Rationale A short explanation generated by the model for why it assigned the topic. Check it against the paper.

docs.title: Downloading the results
docs.text: Download Where What you get Download graph (HTML) Explore The current graph view as an interactive HTML file you can open offline. Download papers (CSV) Papers The extracted paper table, including metadata, abstracts, and references when available. Download papers and topics (JSON) Topics The paper records with their saved topic labels, categories, confidence scores, and rationales.

docs.title: Update or repair a project
docs.text:
Open Project tools and enable Show processing controls when needed:

  • Update graph: supply the PDF folder and select a topic model. New and previously failed PDFs are processed, successful extractions are reused, and topics are generated for the collection with the selected model.
  • Re-extract topics: choose a different model without processing PDFs again. This also completes a project whose paper extraction succeeded but whose topic extraction failed.
  • Rebuild paper table: regenerate metadata tables from saved paper extractions. This does not change the saved topics. If the set of papers has changed, re-extract topics to bring the graph up to date.

If topic extraction fails during an update, the last completed topics remain available. The page warns when those topics cover a different set of papers from the current paper table.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Click a problem to see what to do.

A paper has no topics

Under Papers, use Download papers (CSV) and check the abstract column. Text Lab skips topic extraction if there is no abstract. Also check that Topics is enabled in Advanced graph options. In Whole collection, try lowering Minimum topic confidence to see whether topics were filtered out.

I expected to see a citation between two papers

Turn on Cited papers in Advanced graph options. If the connection is still missing, download the paper table from Papers and check the citing paper's cited_titles column. Grobid may have missed the reference, or its extracted title may differ from the title in your collection.

The graph is too crowded or I lost track of a node

Use Recenter to fit the nodes back into view. Switch to Single paper to focus on one paper, or use Advanced graph options to show fewer papers or hide node types you do not need.

Related papers have different topic labels

Compare their broader categories and read the titles and abstracts to confirm the relationship. Text Lab connects matching topic labels; the model can describe similar ideas with different words. Use Topics to compare the saved labels. If needed, try another model with Re-extract topics.

I changed a PDF, but the graph still shows old information

Check the filename. Text Lab reuses successful PDF extractions by name. To compare the updated paper with the original, give the new PDF a different filename. To build a collection with only the updated version, create a new project with the revised PDF.

docs.title: Data privacy and storage
docs.text:
• For cluster folder input, original PDFs stay where they are. Uploaded PDFs and ZIP contents are staged temporarily and are not copied permanently.
  • Extracted metadata, text, topics and generated graph HTML files stay in the chosen project folder until you delete them. Choose persistent cluster storage if you want to return in another session.
  • Grobid's temporary working copies use the session's private workspace and are deleted when the session ends.
  • With the session model, titles and abstracts are processed in your own job. With GPUStack, they are sent to the University of Bern's service, staying on university infrastructure.

docs.title: How to Launch Text Lab
docs.text: Text Lab runs as an interactive app on the University of Bern's High Performance Computing cluster (UBELIX) via the Open OnDemand portal.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Guide
docs.text:
1. Log in to the UBELIX Open OnDemand Portal.
  2. Navigate to Interactive Apps or Data Science Lab Services and select Text Lab.
  3. You will see a configuration form.

docs.title: Basic Configuration
docs.text:
By default, only the essential options are shown:

Parameter Recommended Setting Description Account gratis or your available account Select the account under which the session should run. Job Time (hours) 1 to 4 Total time you plan to use Text Lab. If the session reaches the selected limit, it will stop automatically. Advanced Slurm Options Unchecked for most users Leave unchecked for standard usage. Enable it only if you need to manually choose GPU and other Slurm settings.

docs.title: Advanced Slurm Options
docs.text:
If you check Advanced Slurm Options, additional parameters will appear.

Parameter Recommended Setting Description SLURM Partition gpu Standard GPU partition for most users. Use gpu-invest only if your account and project require it. Quality of Service (QoS) Depends on your account Choose a QoS that matches your account and partition. For many standard users, job_gratis is the correct choice. GPU Type rtx4090 for most tasks Suitable for most transcription and OCR tasks. Use A100, H100, or H200 only if you need more GPU memory or want to run larger LLMs. Number of GPU(s) requested 1 One GPU is enough for most use cases. Request more than one only for large LLM workloads. wckey Optional Provide a valid project identifier for accounting if needed. This is usually optional when using the gratis account. Reservation Optional Only fill this in if you have been given an active Slurm reservation name, for example for a workshop or course.

docs.title: Notes on QoS and GPU Selection
docs.text:
• job_gratis is typically the default choice for users launching Text Lab with a gratis account.
  • job_gpu or job_gpu_preemptable may be relevant if you are using a specific project allocation.
  • A100 or H100 are recommended only for larger LLM workloads and usually together with job_gpu_preemptable, depending on your account setup.
  • If you are unsure, start with the default settings and only enable advanced options when necessary.

docs.title: Starting the Session
docs.text:
1. Click Launch.
  2. Wait for the job to start. The status will change from Queued to Running.
  3. Click Connect to Text Lab to open the interface in your browser.

docs.title: Reporting a Problem
docs.text:
If something goes wrong in Text Lab, the session's log files help us find out what happened. Each session writes them to its own folder in your home directory:

  1. In Open OnDemand, open My Interactive Sessions.
  2. On the card of the session where the problem happened, click the link next to Session ID. It opens the session folder in the file browser.
  3. Download output.log, streamlit.log and ollama.log.
  4. Send them to support.dsl@unibe.ch, together with the date and time of the problem and what you were doing.

The logs contain technical messages such as errors, file names and model names. An error message can occasionally quote a short piece of the text being processed, so treat the logs as confidentially as your data. They stay in your home directory until you delete the session folder.

docs.title: More Information
docs.text: For more information about Slurm parameters and job configuration on UBELIX, see the UBELIX documentation.

docs.title: Meeting Notes Generator
docs.text:
The Meeting Notes Generator turns a recording into written notes in one step. Upload the audio of a meeting, interview or lecture, and you get back a full transcript together with a structured summary: decisions and action items for a meeting, themes and quotes for an interview, or study notes for a lecture. Each point in the summary shows where in the transcript it comes from, so you can check it. If you already have a transcript, you can summarise it directly.

All processing runs on the university cluster. Your audio and text never leave the university network, and nothing is sent to external services such as OpenAI, Google or Anthropic.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Open the From Audio tab.
  2. Upload your recording under Audio file.
  3. Choose the language spoken in the recording, or keep Auto-detect.
  4. Choose a summary type, for example Meeting Notes.
  5. Click Transcribe and Summarize.
  6. When it is done, read the summary, check its points against the Sources tab, and download the results.

A one-hour recording usually takes several minutes. The page shows each step as it happens.

docs.title: Choosing what to start from
docs.text:
The page has two tabs:

  • From Audio: you have a recording. Text Lab transcribes it and then summarises the transcript.
  • From Transcript: you already have the text, for example a transcript you made on the Transcription page or notes from another source. Only the summary is created, which is much faster.

docs.title: Summary types
docs.text:
The summary type decides what the notes focus on and how they are organised.

Summary type Best for What you get General Summary Any recording A short introduction, a bulleted list of key points and a brief conclusion Meeting Notes Team meetings, project meetings Summary, key decisions, action items (with owner and deadline when they were mentioned), topics discussed and participants Interview Summary Interviews, focus groups, conversations Overview, main themes, key statements and notable quotes, conclusions Academic Abstract Talks and presentations about research Background and objective, methods, findings, conclusions and implications Lecture Notes Lectures and seminars Lecture overview, topics covered, key concepts and definitions, important examples, summary

You can try another type later without transcribing the recording again (see Changing settings after a run). Whatever the type, each point shows where in the transcript it comes from.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• Audio file: .wav, .mp3, .flac, .m4a, .ogg or .webm. One file at a time.
  • Language: the language spoken in the recording.
    • Auto-detect listens to the first 30 seconds and picks the language. The detected language and how confident the detection was are shown as the first step. If the recording starts with silence, music or a different language, choose the language yourself.
    • Swiss German and Swiss German (Flurin Turbo) use models trained on Swiss German dialects. Auto-detect never picks these, so select one of them yourself for Swiss German recordings. See Transcription for details.
  • Summary type: see Summary types.
  • Summary language:
    • English writes the summary in English, whatever language was spoken.
    • Transcript language writes the summary in the language of the recording.
  • Summarization model: the language model that writes the summary. If you are unsure, keep the first one. Which models are offered depends on the GPU of your Text Lab session: in Standard mode large models are hidden, in High-performance mode all models are available.
  • Speaker diarization settings (optional): if you know how many people speak in the recording, tick Set minimum speakers and Set maximum speakers and enter the numbers. This helps Text Lab tell the voices apart. For an interview with two people, set both to 2.

GPU memory in use

If you used another Text Lab feature earlier in the session, a warning may say that models are still loaded in GPU memory. Click Clear GPU Memory before you start, so the transcription has enough memory.

docs.title: Running
docs.text:
Click Transcribe and Summarize. The page then shows each step:

  1. Detecting language (only with Auto-detect).
  2. Running transcription pipeline: the audio is converted, transcribed, aligned word by word, and split by speaker.
  3. Generating summary: the first run loads the language model into GPU memory, which can take 1–2 minutes.

To cancel a run, reload the page.

docs.title: Naming the speakers
docs.text:
The transcript labels the voices it finds as SPEAKER_00, SPEAKER_01 and so on. To replace these labels with real names or roles:

  1. Once the transcription is done, open Name the speakers (optional) below the Transcribe and Summarize button.
  2. Type a name for each speaker, for example Interviewer and Participant, or the people's names.
  3. Click Re-summarize with current settings.

The first summary is created right after the transcription, before you can enter names. It still uses the SPEAKER_00 labels, and a notice appears once you have entered names. Clicking Re-summarize creates a new summary, sources and transcript download that use your names. The recording is not transcribed again.

Finding out who is who

Open the Full Transcript tab and read the first few lines of each speaker to work out who they are. You can also listen to a passage in the Sources tab (see Checking the summary against the transcript). Speaker separation is automatic and can make mistakes, especially with similar voices, people talking over each other, or poor audio.

docs.title: Changing settings after a run
docs.text:
After a run you can change the summary type, summary language, model or speaker names and click Re-summarize with current settings. Only the summary is created again, which is much faster than the first run. A notice reminds you when the summary shown no longer matches your current settings.

If you upload a different file or change the language, the recording has to be transcribed again: click Transcribe and Summarize.

docs.title: If the summary fails
docs.text: If something goes wrong while the summary is written, the page shows the error, and the transcript stays available to read and download. Click Retry summarization to try again without transcribing the recording again. If it keeps failing, try a different model, or click Clear GPU Memory first. Open Error details to see the full message if you need to report the problem.

docs.title: From Transcript
docs.text:
1. Open the From Transcript tab.

  2. Choose an Input method:

    • Upload transcript CSV (from Transcribe page): the CSV download from the Transcription page. Speaker labels are kept, and you can name the speakers under Name the speakers (optional).
    • Upload text file: a plain .txt file.
    • Paste text: paste the transcript into the text box.

    If the text has the labels SPEAKER_00, SPEAKER_01 and so on at the start of its lines, you can name the speakers here too. 3. Check the word count shown below the input to make sure the whole text was read. 4. Choose the summary type, model and summary language. 5. Click Generate Summary.

The summary stays on the page while you download files. If you then change the text or the settings, a notice reminds you to click Generate Summary again.

Better summaries from pasted text

If your text has speaker names at the start of each line (for example Anna: I think we should...), the summary can say who said what and who owns each action item.

The summary cites the lines of your text, so keep one statement or speaker turn per line. Very long lines, such as text pasted without line breaks, are split into sentences.

docs.title: Results and downloads
docs.text:
At the top, the results show the summary type, the number of words in the transcript and, for audio, the length of the recording. Three tabs show the Summary, its Sources and the Full Transcript.

Each line of the transcript starts with a label: the time it was said, such as [05:12], or its line number, such as [12], for text without timestamps. The summary uses the same labels to show where each point comes from (see Checking the summary against the transcript).

Downloads:

  • Summary (.md): the notes only. The sources are footnotes: each point is followed by a reference such as [^12], and the footnotes at the end quote the transcript lines with their time and speaker.
  • Transcript (.txt): the transcript, one line per segment, with its time or line number and with speaker names if you set them.
  • Full document (.md): the summary with its footnotes and the full transcript in one file, with the file name and summary type at the top.

From Audio also offers Download raw transcription files:

  • Transcript CSV (WhisperX): each segment with start and end time and speaker. You can upload this file again later on the From Transcript tab.
  • Plain transcript (.txt): the text only, without speaker labels.

.md files are Markdown: plain text with simple formatting such as **bold** and - lists. They open in any text editor, and Word, Obsidian, Notion and most note apps can import them.

Results are kept only while the page is open. Download everything you want to keep before you reload the page, close the browser tab or end your Text Lab session.

docs.title: Long recordings
docs.text: Recordings of several hours are supported. When a transcript is too long for the model to read at once (roughly 12,000 words, about one and a half hours of conversation), it is split into parts. Notes are taken for each part, and then the notes are combined into one summary. You see the progress as Analyzing part 2 of 5... and then Synthesizing final summary.... This takes longer than a single pass, and small details are more likely to be left out. The sources are kept through every step, so the summary of a long recording cites the transcript too.

docs.title: Checking the summary against the transcript
docs.text:
The model is asked to cite, after every point, the transcript lines it is based on. Text Lab then checks these citations against the transcript:

  • In the Summary tab, each point ends with grey labels such as (05:12, 06:40): the times (or line numbers) of the lines it is based on. A note above the summary says how many lines are cited.
  • Points marked (no source) in orange cite nothing. Check these first: they may be a general remark, or something the model added.
  • Citations of lines that do not exist are removed, and the note above the summary says how many. Many removed citations mean the model struggled; try another model.
  • The Sources tab lists every cited line with its time, speaker and text. For a recording, choose a passage under Listen to a cited passage to play the audio from that moment.
  • If the summary cites nothing at all, a warning says so. Some models do not follow the instruction; try another one.

A citation shows where a point comes from, not that the point is right: the model can still misread a line. Before you share or act on the notes:

  • Check names, numbers and dates against the cited lines. Speech recognition often mishears names and technical terms.
  • Check action items and decisions. The model may miss one, or give it to the wrong person, especially when speaker labels are wrong.
  • Use the Full Transcript tab to read the context around a cited line.

The model is told to use only what is in the transcript and not to add information. It can still make mistakes.

docs.title: Data privacy and security
docs.text:
Recordings of meetings and interviews often contain personal or confidential information. This is what happens to your data:

  • Everything runs on the university cluster. Transcription (WhisperX) and summarisation (language models served by Ollama) run on the UBELIX compute node of your Text Lab session. No audio or text is sent to an external service.
  • Temporary files are deleted after transcription. For transcription, your audio is written to a temporary folder in your session's private workspace on the compute node, together with the progress and result files. The folder is deleted as soon as the transcription ends, whether it succeeded or failed, and the whole workspace is deleted when your session ends.
  • Results live only in your browser session. The transcript and summary are kept in your open page only. They are not saved to your home directory, and they are gone when you reload the page, close the tab or your Text Lab session ends.
  • No AI training. The models only process your recording. They do not learn from it, and your data is never used to train or improve them.

docs.title: Optical Character Recognition (OCR)
docs.text: The OCR tool extracts editable text, tables, figures, and formulas from scanned PDFs or images, and preserves the document's layout in a structured result. Optional local analysis can describe figures.

docs.title: Supported Input
docs.text:
• Documents: PDF (.pdf). Note: For multi-page PDFs, processing may take a while per page depending on layout density.
  • Images: PNG, JPG, JPEG, BMP, TIFF
  • Archives: ZIP (.zip) (for batch processing multiple documents or images at once).

docs.title: Automatic mode (default)
docs.text:
The recommended workflow is fully automatic — there is no engine, language, or mode to choose. Just upload a file and press Parse document.

Under the hood, Text Lab:

  • Detects layout with a single multilingual model (PaddleOCR-VL, 109 languages), classifying every region as text, title, table, image/chart, formula, footnote, header/footer, seal, or checkbox.
  • Reads structure, not just text: tables become spreadsheets, formulas become LaTeX, and figures are cropped out.
  • Takes a fast lane for born-digital PDFs: pages that already contain a real text layer are read directly (no AI vision needed); only scanned/image pages go through the vision model.
  • Optionally describes detected figures/images with Text Lab's local vision-language model. Generated descriptions and visible-text transcriptions remain separate from printed OCR content.

Results are shown in tabs:

  • Document — the full text rendered in reading order, with tables, figures, and formulas inline.
  • Tables — each detected table as an interactive spreadsheet, with a per-table CSV download.
  • Figures — cropped images, charts, and seals, plus generated descriptions when requested.
  • Layout preview — the page image with colour-coded boxes for each region type.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
• Searchable PDF: the original pages, unchanged to the eye, with an invisible text layer so the scan becomes selectable and searchable. Produced automatically for a single document; for a batch it is a tick-box, since the cost multiplies by the number of files. The indexed text is Text Lab's own OCR result — Tesseract runs a second pass purely to locate each word, and never overrides what was transcribed. Table cells are included, since they really are printed; formulas are left out, because the exported LaTeX is not what the reader sees. Tables align less precisely than prose — the reading order of a grid and of flowing text do not always agree — so a mis-set cell stays searchable but highlights a wider span.

    The document language is detected automatically, per page, from the text Text Lab already extracted, so mixed-language documents are handled page by page. It only affects how precisely each word is positioned: on a scanned German questionnaire, using deu placed 87.6% of words on their exact box against 82.1% for eng. Pages with too little text keep the English default, and you can always set the language explicitly. * Plain text (.txt): the text in reading order, with tables rendered as aligned columns and no markup. Best for text analysis or pasting elsewhere. * Word (.docx): an editable document with real headings, Word tables, and embedded figures — for revising or citing the result. * Markdown + assets (.zip): clean Markdown with the cropped figures alongside. Best for LLM/RAG ingestion. * JSON: the canonical structured representation (regions, bounding boxes, confidence, markup states) for developers and further analysis. * Tables (.csv .zip): one CSV per detected table. * Full bundle (.zip): Markdown, plain text, .docx, JSON, assets, and table CSVs together.

Formats are generated from the same structured result, so they always agree; nothing is re-OCR'd per download.

docs.title: Which models produced the result (for citation)
docs.text:
Expand Models used (for citation) under the downloads to see exactly which models ran on your document. The same summary is written as models_used.txt in the bundle, once at the root of a batch result, and as a models block in each document's JSON. It is read off what actually ran rather than restated, so it stays correct if the configured models change:

  • Text recognition — PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 (PaddleOCR 3.7 / PaddleX 3.7) for scanned pages and images. Born-digital pages taken by the fast lane report PyMuPDF text extraction (no recognition model), because no recognition model is involved in reading an existing text layer.
  • Figure descriptions — the local vision-language model, by name and tag (by default qwen3-vl:30b-a3b-instruct, served through Ollama), listed only when descriptions were actually generated.
  • Searchable-PDF word geometry — Tesseract, with its version and the language pack used. It supplies word positions only and never contributes text.

When quoting results in a publication, keep the distinction: printed text is transcribed by the recognition model, while figure descriptions are generated by a vision-language model and are not part of the source document.

docs.title: Batch processing (ZIP)
docs.text: Choose Batch OCR (ZIP), upload a .zip of PDFs/images, and press Parse batch. The result ZIP mirrors your original folder structure and each file gets every format the single-document page offers, written by the same code: document.md, document.txt, document.docx, document.json, document_searchable.pdf (when the tick-box is set), plus tables/ and assets/ folders. A single models_used.txt sits at the root of the result rather than in every folder, listing every model that ran anywhere in the batch — a batch can mix scans and born-digital PDFs, which take different lanes.

docs.title: Survey/form response extraction (not enabled)
docs.text: A question-level survey/form response extractor is present in the codebase but switched off in the interface while it is validated against a representative multi-document benchmark. It renders complete 300-DPI question sections to the local vision-language model, assigns its own IDs, verifies each marked position against an echoed choice label, derives selection constraints independently, and flags empty or inconsistent responses; OCR text and table HTML are never modified by it. Developers can reach it through OcrOptions(extract_survey=True) in textlab.features.ocr.service, or re-expose the UI controls, the Responses tab, and the form-responses CSV by setting SURVEY_EXTRACTION_UI_ENABLED = True in src/textlab/ui/streamlit/ocr/state.py.

docs.title: Advanced: legacy engines
docs.text:
The previous engine-picker workflow is still available under the “Advanced: legacy engines” expander for cases where you want a specific engine's plain-text output:

  1. EasyOCR: general-purpose text across many languages.
  2. PaddleOCR: strong on complex or multi-column layouts.
  3. OlmOCR: tuned for converting scientific PDFs into clean Markdown.
  4. GLM-OCR: a large vision model with selectable Text / Table / Figure extraction modes.

Each legacy engine returns plain text (or Markdown) per page. For most documents — and for anything with tables or checkboxes — the automatic mode above is recommended.

The downloads of a single document are the whole text (.txt), the engine's result with positions and scores (.json; OlmOCR gives its own .jsonl record), and a ZIP with both plus one text and JSON file per page. In a batch, each file gets a folder with the same files, mirroring your ZIP's folders. If an engine fails on one file, the batch stops with an error naming it.

Warning: Do not close the tab while a "Running" indicator is active.

docs.title: Historic German handwriting
docs.text: The "Historic German handwriting (Kurrent / medieval manuscripts)" expander, below the legacy engines, transcribes handwritten historical German documents such as letters, minutes and charters. It uses handwriting recognition models of the Digital Humanities group of the University of Bern (dh-unibe), trained specifically on such material. The rest of the OCR page is unaffected, and the two keep their results apart.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
Choose the model trained on material closest to your documents. The Models used box under the model choice shows, before you upload anything, which models will process your documents, with links to their pages on Hugging Face.

Choice in Text Lab Model Trained on Character error rate German Kurrent, 19th century dh-unibe/qwen3vl-german-xix-v2 Handwritten German in Kurrent script, 19th century, mainly Swiss records such as Federal Council minutes and parliamentary protocols 7.7% on hands it has not seen (Federal Council minutes 1848-1903) Medieval German, 14th-17th century dh-unibe/qwen3vl-medieval-german-v3 Medieval and early modern German hands: the Rats- und Richtebücher, the Bullinger correspondence, the Königsfelden charters and the AAEB collections about 14%

Both are fine-tuned versions (LoRA adapters) of the vision-language model Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct. The text lines are found by the baseline segmenter of kraken (blla, its default model), which was trained on historical manuscripts.

A character error rate of 7.7% means that about one character in thirteen is wrong; 14% is about one in seven.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Find the lines. kraken finds every text line on each page, also slanted or curved ones, and puts the lines in reading order. It first finds the text regions, such as columns and marginal notes, and orders the lines region by region.
  2. Read each line. The chosen model reads every line separately. The models were trained on single lines and cannot read a whole page at once, which is why the page is split first.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
• Input: PDF (rendered at 300 DPI), PNG, JPG, JPEG, TIFF (every page of a multi-page TIFF) and BMP, or a ZIP of these. Scans at 300 DPI or more give the best results.
  • Single document: upload a file and press Transcribe. The result shows, page by page, the image with the detected lines outlined and numbered, next to the numbered transcription.
  • Batch (ZIP): upload a .zip and press Transcribe batch. The result ZIP mirrors your folders, with one folder per file.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
• Text (.txt): one line per detected line, pages separated by a blank line.
  • JSON: every line with its position on the page (in pixels of the page image).
  • All files with PAGE XML (.zip): the text and JSON, plus one PAGE XML file per page in page_xml/, which can be imported into eScriptorium or Transkribus to correct the transcription against the image. For a PDF or a multi-page TIFF the page images the positions refer to are included next to the XML; for a single image the XML refers to your uploaded file.
  • Citation: models_used.txt in the ZIP, and Models used (for citation) under the downloads, name the line detector and the recognition model with the base model it adapts, for example dh-unibe/qwen3vl-german-xix-v2 (LoRA adapter on Qwen/Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Treat the result as a draft to correct, not as an edition.

  • Errors are expected. The error rates above were measured on the models' test material; on hands, scribes or periods unlike the training data they are higher. The models are language models, so a wrong reading can still look like fluent, plausible German. Check names, numbers and dates against the image in particular.
  • German historical handwriting only. The models were trained on 19th-century Kurrent and on medieval and early modern German hands. They are not meant for print, modern handwriting or other languages; use the automatic mode above for those.
  • Check the detected lines. kraken was trained on manuscripts, but it can still miss faint or very short lines, split a line in two, or join lines that touch, most often in dense writing. A missed line is missing from the text, and two lines detected as one are read as one, so compare the outlined, numbered lines with the page.
  • Reading order, no further layout. Lines are ordered region by region, which usually keeps columns and marginal notes apart. On unusual layouts the order can still be wrong, and interlinear additions are placed by their position, not by where they belong in the text. Paragraphs, tables, headings and figures are not recognised.
  • No context between lines. Each line is read on its own, so a word hyphenated across two lines is not joined, and the model cannot use the previous line to resolve an unclear word.
  • Transcription conventions. Abbreviations, special characters and spelling follow the conventions of the training transcriptions, which may differ from your editorial guidelines.
  • No confidence scores and no searchable PDF. Unlike the automatic mode, there is no per-word confidence and no searchable PDF export.
  • Speed. Every run first loads the model onto the GPU, which takes about a minute; after that, a page takes a few seconds. A large batch can take a long time.

docs.title: Hugging Face OCR models (choose your own model)
docs.text: The Hugging Face OCR models expander, below historic handwriting, reads documents with a vision-language model you choose from Hugging Face, for example a model fine-tuned on a script, a language or a kind of document that the built-in tools do not cover. It is separate from the rest of the OCR page and does not change it.

docs.title: Use
docs.text:
1. Enter the model as owner/name (for example Qwen/Qwen2.5-VL-3B-Instruct) or paste the link to its page. A link to the model's page appears below; read its model card.
  2. Prompt: the instruction sent with every page. A model trained with a specific prompt reads best with that one; its model card usually names it. Leave the field empty for models that take no instruction.
  3. Most tokens per page: the upper limit of the text generated for one page. A dense page needs about 1,000 to 2,000; lower it if a model keeps repeating itself.
  4. Upload a PDF or image (Single document) or a ZIP of them (Batch (ZIP)) and press Read document or Read batch. The model reads each page as a whole.

The first run with a model downloads it, which can take several minutes for a large one; later runs only load it onto the GPU.

docs.title: Which models work
docs.text:
• Vision-language models that Transformers supports directly, listed on Hugging Face under Image-Text-to-Text: for example the Qwen2.5-VL and Qwen3-VL families and models fine-tuned from them (such as olmOCR), or SmolVLM. Text Lab treats every model the same way, so how well a model reads depends on the model; try it on a few pages first.
  • Not supported, with a message before anything is downloaded or loaded:
    • models that need code from their own repository (the model card asks for trust_remote_code=True), because Text Lab does not run code from model repositories;
    • gated models, which require accepting conditions with a Hugging Face account, and private models: Text Lab downloads only public models, without an account;
    • adapters (LoRA) published without their base model merged in: Text Lab loads full models only;
    • models too large for the GPU of your session. A model needs about 2 GB of GPU memory per billion parameters, so on a 24 GB GPU models up to about 9 billion parameters fit.
  • Some models need Python packages that Text Lab's image does not have yet; the error message then names the package. Tell the Text Lab team, who can add it.

docs.title: Your downloaded models
docs.text: Models are downloaded into your own folder, ~/.cache/textlab/hf_ocr_models in your home directory, not into Text Lab's shared model store. They count towards your storage quota and can take several GB each. Your downloaded models lists them with their size; delete one you no longer need, and it is downloaded again on its next use.

docs.title: Downloads
docs.text:
• Text (.txt): the text of every page, pages separated by a blank line.
  • JSON: the text page by page, with the model and the prompt.
  • All files (.zip): both, plus model_used.txt. A batch gives one folder per file, mirroring the ZIP.
  • Citation: Model used (for citation) and model_used.txt name the model with the exact revision that was downloaded, and the prompt.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Check the output. A vision-language model can leave out text, repeat it or invent plausible text that is not on the page, more so for handwriting, damaged pages or scripts it was not trained on.
  • Text only. The result is the text the model writes, often in Markdown or HTML for tables. There are no positions on the page, no PAGE XML, no confidence scores and no searchable PDF.
  • The model's license applies. You are responsible for using the model and its output as its license allows.

docs.title: Data Privacy & Security
docs.text:
Text Lab is designed to handle highly sensitive, confidential, and proprietary documents (including unredacted PDFs, medical records, or unpublished manuscripts). We utilize a strict "Local-Only, Self-Cleaning" architecture to ensure your documents remain secure.

Here is exactly what happens to your data when you use the OCR tool:

  • 100% Local Processing: Your documents are never sent to external cloud services or APIs (like Adobe, Google Cloud Vision, or AWS). All text extraction is performed entirely on the University of Bern's secure UBELIX high-performance computing nodes.
  • Private session workspace: The automatic pipeline, advanced AI vision models (like OlmOCR), historic German handwriting, and Batch ZIP processing all need to read files from disk (uploads, rasterised pages, cropped regions and line crops). Text Lab keeps these in a private workspace that is created for your session on the compute node and that only your user account can open. Your documents are never written to your home directory; the only thing stored there is a model you choose in the Hugging Face OCR models tool.
  • Automatic deletion: As soon as the extraction finishes, or fails, the working folder of that run is deleted, including your original documents, intermediate images and raw data files. If a run is interrupted, for example because the session ends, the whole session workspace is deleted when the session ends.
  • Results in your browser session: The extracted text and tables shown on the page are kept only in your open session (Streamlit's st.session_state). When you close the tab, reload the page, or your Text Lab session ends, they are gone. Download anything you want to keep.
  • No AI Training: The vision models only perform inference (looking at the image to extract text). They do not learn from your documents, and your data is never used to train or improve the AI.

docs.title: Topic Modeling
docs.text:
Topic Modeling finds the main themes in a collection of texts automatically. You upload your documents, and Text Lab groups documents that talk about similar things into topics, describes each topic with its most characteristic keywords, and tells you which topic every document belongs to.

Typical uses are exploring survey answers, interview transcripts, news articles, social media posts, abstracts, or any other collection that is too large to read in full.

All processing runs on the university cluster. Your documents are never sent to an external service.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Upload your data as a table (CSV or Excel) or as a ZIP archive of text files.
  2. Pick the column that contains the text (tables only).
  3. Choose an algorithm. If you are unsure, start with BERTopic and the default settings.
  4. Select the primary language of your texts.
  5. Click Run Topic Extraction. A status box shows each step; to cancel, refresh the page. Notes about the run, such as skipped rows or long documents, appear when it finishes.
  6. Explore the results on the page and click Download Extraction Package (.zip) to keep them.

Running again with different settings replaces the previous results on the page, so download anything you want to keep first.

docs.title: Preparing your data
docs.text: Each document is one unit that gets assigned to a topic: one table row or one text file.

docs.title: Tables (recommended)
docs.text:
• Formats: CSV (.csv) or Excel (.xlsx). Older .xls files are not supported; open them in Excel and save them as .xlsx or .csv.
  • Use one row per document and one column for the text. All other columns (author, date, category, ...) are kept and appear in the exported results next to the assigned topic, so you can analyse topics by group later.
  • CSV files may use commas, semicolons, tabs or pipes as separators, and may be saved by Excel on Windows. Text Lab detects both automatically.
  • Rows with an empty text cell are skipped.

docs.title: ZIP archives
docs.text:
• Put plain text files (.txt) into a ZIP archive, one document per file. Up to 1,000 files are accepted.
  • The file name is kept and appears in the exported results.
  • Use this when your documents are separate files; use a table if you also have metadata.

docs.title: Tips for good results
docs.text:
• Choose a sensible document size. Topic models work best when each document is about one thing: an answer, a paragraph, an abstract or an article. A whole book as one document usually mixes many themes; consider splitting it into chapters or paragraphs.
  • More is better. At least 5 documents are required, but meaningful topics usually need a few hundred. For small collections, use LDA.
  • Remove boilerplate such as email signatures, page headers or legal notices, or add the words as custom stopwords (see below).

docs.title: Choosing an algorithm
docs.text:
BERTopic Top2Vec LDA How it works Uses a language model to understand the meaning of each document, then groups similar documents Learns word and document meanings together, then groups similar documents Counts which words occur together in documents Best for Most use cases; short and medium texts; many languages Medium to large collections Small collections; when you want a classic, well-known method Number of topics Found automatically, or set by you Found automatically, or set by you Always set by you Documents that fit no topic Marked as Outlier (HDBSCAN) Always assigned to the closest topic Always assigned to the most likely topic Topics over time Yes No No Speed Fast; the language model runs on the GPU Slower, especially with deep-learn Fast for small and medium collections

Not sure? Start with BERTopic

BERTopic with the default settings gives good topics for most collections. If it reports that it could not find any topics, your collection is probably too small: switch to LDA.

docs.title: Settings for all algorithms
docs.text:
• Primary Language decides which built-in list of common words (stopwords such as "the", "and", "der", "und") is removed, and which language model BERTopic uses by default.
    • English, German and French: full support, including word base forms for LDA (for example "studies" and "studied" both count as "study").
    • Spanish, Italian, Dutch, Portuguese, Russian and Arabic: built-in stopword lists.
    • Chinese: use BERTopic, which splits Chinese text into words. LDA and Top2Vec do not handle Chinese well.
    • Other / Mixed: uses a multilingual model, without a built-in stopword list.
  • Custom Stopwords (BERTopic and LDA): a comma-separated list of words that should never appear as topic keywords, for example words that occur everywhere in your collection (patient, report, interview). Not available for Top2Vec.
  • Evaluate Topic Stability / Reproducibility (in Academic Evaluation Metrics): runs the model three times and measures how similar the topics are. Useful to check whether your topics are robust, but the run takes about three times as long.

docs.title: BERTopic
docs.text:
Core settings

  • Clustering Engine
    • HDBSCAN (default) finds the number of topics itself and sets aside documents that do not fit any topic as Outlier.
    • KMeans puts every document into exactly the number of topics you choose. There are no outliers.
  • Auto-detect optimal number of topics (HDBSCAN): keep this on to let BERTopic merge very similar topics automatically. Turn it off to ask for a target number of topics.
  • Minimum Documents per Topic (HDBSCAN): the smallest group of documents that counts as a topic. Lower it to get more, smaller topics; raise it to get fewer, broader ones.

Embedding Model

The embedding model is the language model that reads your documents. The defaults work well and are already available on the cluster:

  • English: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, which reads up to 256 tokens (roughly 190 words) per document.
  • Other languages: paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2, which reads up to 128 tokens (roughly 95 words) per document.

If your documents are longer than this, Text Lab shows a warning, because by default the model only reads the beginning of each document. You have two options:

  • Embed long documents in chunks: tick this box to have each long document split into pieces that fit the model, read piece by piece, and combined. The whole document then shapes its topic. This takes longer for long documents.
  • Use a model with a larger context window: choose Custom HuggingFace model and enter a model ID such as jinaai/jina-embeddings-v2-base-en, BAAI/bge-m3 or nomic-ai/nomic-embed-text-v1.5 (about 8,000 tokens each). The model is downloaded to your home directory the first time.
    • Some models (Jina, Nomic) need Allow custom code from this model repository. Only tick it for models from sources you trust, because their code runs under your account.

Text Extraction & Vocabulary

  • Extract Phrases (N-grams): also consider two-word phrases such as "climate change" as keywords.
  • Minimum Topic Frequency (min_df): a word is only used as a keyword if it appears in at least this many topics. Keep it at 1 unless the run runs out of memory on a very large collection; higher values remove the words that make topics distinctive.
  • Auto-penalize frequent words: reduces the weight of words that appear in almost every topic. Keep it on.

Dimensionality Reduction

Leave UMAP selected unless you have a reason to change it. Lock Seed for Reproducibility (on by default) makes repeated runs with the same settings give the same topics.

Clustering & Outliers (HDBSCAN)

  • Outlier Sensitivity (min_samples): lower values put fewer documents into Outlier.
  • Force-assign outliers to nearest topics: assigns every outlier to its closest topic, so no document is left without a topic. Topic sizes and keywords are updated accordingly.

docs.title: Top2Vec
docs.text:
• Auto-detect optimal number of topics: keep this on, or turn it off and choose a target number. If you ask for more topics than Top2Vec finds, it keeps the topics it found.
  • Embedding Backend
    • Transformer (Pre-trained): uses a ready-made language model. Faster, and works well for general language.
    • Doc2Vec (Train from scratch): learns from your documents only. Can capture specialised vocabulary but needs a larger collection.
  • Training Depth: fast-learn, learn or deep-learn. Deeper training can give better topics with Doc2Vec but takes longer.
  • Minimum Word Count (min_count): words that appear fewer times than this in the whole collection are ignored. Lower it for small collections or if Top2Vec finds no topics; raise it to ignore rare words in large collections.

Top2Vec results can differ slightly between runs, even with the same settings.

docs.title: LDA
docs.text:
• Number of Topics: LDA always produces exactly this many topics. Try a few values (for example 5, 10 and 20) and compare the results.
  • Extract Phrases (Bigrams): also consider frequent two-word phrases, which appear as keywords joined by an underscore (climate_change).
  • Training Passes: more passes give more stable topics but take longer. The default of 10 is fine for most collections.

docs.title: Topics over time (BERTopic)
docs.text:
To see how topics rise and fall over time, upload a table, tick Analyze Topics Over Time next to the text column, then:

  • Timestamp Column: a column with dates (2021-03-15), date-times, or whole years (2021).
  • Number of Time Bins: how many time intervals to split the period into. If your data has fewer distinct dates than that (for example five years), each date is shown as its own point.

Rows whose date cannot be read are skipped, and Text Lab tells you how many.

docs.title: Evaluation metrics
docs.text:
The scores at the top help you compare runs on the same data, for example two numbers of topics. They are not absolute quality grades, and they never replace reading the topics yourself.

Metric What it tells you Better Topic Diversity How different the topics' keywords are from each other Higher Coherence (C_v) How often a topic's keywords appear together in your documents; the measure that best matches human judgement Higher (0 to 1) Coherence (C_npmi) A related co-occurrence measure Higher (-1 to 1) Coherence (U_mass) A co-occurrence measure based on document counts Closer to 0 LDA Perplexity (LDA only) How well the model predicts the documents it was trained on Lower Topic Stability (if enabled) How similar the topics are across three runs Higher (100% = identical)

A metric shows N/A when it cannot be computed for a run, for example when too few keywords occur in the documents. Expand How are these scores computed? on the page for details.

docs.title: Topic Dictionary
docs.text:
The table lists every topic with:

  • Topic: the topic number. The same numbers are used in all charts and in the exported files.
  • Count: how many documents belong to the topic (BERTopic and Top2Vec).
  • Keywords: the ten words that best characterise the topic. Read them together to give the topic a name.

Documents marked as Outlier (BERTopic with HDBSCAN) are not listed as a topic, but they appear in the exported document table.

docs.title: Interactive charts
docs.text:
• BERTopic
    • Intertopic Distance: each circle is a topic, larger circles hold more documents, and topics close to each other are similar. Use the slider to highlight a topic.
    • Word Scores: the most important keywords of the largest topics.
    • Similarity Heatmap: how similar every pair of topics is. Dark squares away from the diagonal point to topics you might merge.
    • Topics Over Time: how often each topic appears in each time interval, if you enabled it.
  • Top2Vec: the most characteristic words of the largest topics.
  • LDA: an interactive map of topics on the left and the keywords of the selected topic on the right. Move the relevance slider towards 0 to see words that are specific to the selected topic.

docs.title: Downloading the results
docs.text:
Download Extraction Package (.zip) contains:

  • document_topics.csv: your original data with two new columns at the front.
    • Dominant_Topic: the topic of each document, or Outlier.
    • Topic_Confidence: how strongly the document belongs to that topic; higher means a clearer match. It is empty when BERTopic uses KMeans or force-assigned outliers.
  • topic_keywords.csv: the Topic Dictionary.
  • run_configuration.txt: every setting and score of the run. Keep it with your results so that you can report and reproduce your analysis.
  • The interactive charts as .html files, which open in any web browser. They need an internet connection to display.

The CSV files use commas as separators. If Excel shows everything in one column, import the file with Data > From Text/CSV instead of double-clicking it. If you used topics over time, the rows are sorted by date, and rows without a valid date are left out.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Click a problem to see what to do.

'BERTopic/Top2Vec could not find any topics in these documents'

The collection is too small or too uniform to form groups. Add more documents or switch to LDA.

Many documents are marked as Outlier

Lower Minimum Documents per Topic or Outlier Sensitivity, tick Force-assign outliers to nearest topics, or switch the clustering engine to KMeans.

Too many or too few topics

BERTopic: change Minimum Documents per Topic, or turn off auto-detection and set a target number. LDA: change Number of Topics.

Keywords are full of generic words

Add them to Custom Stopwords, keep Auto-penalize frequent words on, and check that the Primary Language matches your texts.

'No topic keywords could be extracted with a Minimum Topic Frequency ...'

Set Minimum Topic Frequency (min_df) back to 1.

Top2Vec finds no topics on a small collection

Lower Minimum Word Count (min_count), use the Transformer backend, or switch to LDA.

Warning that documents exceed the context window

Tick Embed long documents in chunks, or choose a model with a larger context window (see Embedding Model).

'The timestamp column contains numbers that are not years'

Number columns are only read as whole years (2021). Use a column with real dates, or convert numeric dates such as 20210315 to 2021-03-15.

The embedding model cannot be loaded

Check the model ID on huggingface.co. If the message mentions custom code, tick Allow custom code from this model repository (for trusted models only).

Results change between runs

For BERTopic, keep Lock Seed for Reproducibility on. LDA always uses a fixed seed. Top2Vec cannot be fixed, so small differences are expected.

For help choosing settings for your project, contact the Data Science Lab (DSL).

docs.title: Transcription Service
docs.text: The Transcription tool uses WhisperX to convert spoken audio into written text with precise timestamps and speaker identification.

docs.title: Supported Formats
docs.text:
You can upload audio files in the following formats:

  • .wav
  • .mp3
  • .flac
  • .m4a
  • .zip (for batch processing multiple audio files at once)

docs.title: Single Audio Transcription
docs.text:
1. Select Workflow: Choose "Transcribe audio".
  2. Upload File: Drag and drop your audio file.
  3. Language Selection:
  4. The system will attempt to auto-detect the language.
  5. Important: You must verify or manually select the correct language from the dropdown.

docs.title: Batch Processing (Multiple Files)
docs.text:
If you have multiple audio recordings (e.g., a folder of 10 interviews), you can transcribe them all in one go without clicking through them individually:

  1. Select Workflow: Choose "Batch transcribe (ZIP)".
  2. Upload File: Compress all your audio files into a single .zip archive on your computer and upload it.
  3. Language Selection: * You can choose a specific language to force the AI to use that language for all files.
  4. Alternatively, select Auto-detect. The AI will dynamically analyze and figure out the correct language for each file individually before transcribing it.
  5. Process: Click Start. The AI will load the models once and loop through your entire ZIP file at maximum speed.

docs.title: Swiss German Support
docs.text:
Text Lab includes a specialized fine-tuned model for Swiss German.

  • Select Swiss German from the language list.
  • This uses the swhisper-large-1.1 model, which achieves a Word Error Rate (WER) of approximately 18, significantly outperforming standard models on Swiss German dialects. More info about the fine-tuned whisper will be published soon.

The model (Flurin17/whisper-large-v3-turbo-swiss-german) is also available on Text Lab when selecting "Swiss German (Flurin Turbo)". More info on the model in the link

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
• VAD (Voice Activity Detection) (Optional):
  • Check this to filter out silence before processing.
  • Max Pause: Determines how much silence is allowed between words before splitting a segment.
  • Speaker Diarization (Who is speaking?):
  • Text Lab labels each speaker (SPEAKER_00, SPEAKER_01, ...) with pyannote's speaker-diarization-community-1 model, the newer successor of the 3.1 model used before November 2026 and better at telling voices apart.
  • Min/Max Speakers (Optional): If you know how many people are in the recording, set these numbers to help the AI distinguish between voices (e.g., for an interview, set Min=2, Max=2).

docs.title: Results & Export
docs.text:
Once the transcription is complete, you can:

  • Preview (Single Files Only): Listen to the audio with a synchronized interactive text player.
